title: Constant-delay conjunctive-query classification
area: Database theory and finite model theory
formal: Is there a total algorithm that, given any conjunctive query q with self-joins allowed, decides whether q admits enumeration of all distinct answers with \(O_{q}(N)\) preprocessing and \(O_{q}(1)\) worst-case delay on every database of size N?
definitions: A query is a finite formula \(q(\bar\{x\})=\exists \bar\{y\} \land _{i} R_{i}(\bar\{z\}_{i})\), with no constants, negation, disequalities or aggregation. The head x̄ lists distinct variables; every variable occurs in a relational atom. Relation symbols have fixed positive finite arities within q and may occur repeatedly; repeated variables within atoms are allowed. Boolean queries have an empty head. A database D explicitly lists finite set-valued relations over a domain \([n]; N=1+n\)+the total number of tuple entries in these lists. Each domain identifier fits in \(O(\log (N+2))\) bits. \(q(D)\) is the set of head tuples extendible to an assignment satisfying all atoms. Fix the deterministic word-RAM convention with addition, multiplication, comparison, Boolean word operations and indirect access costing one step, words of \(O_{q}(\log (N+2))\) bits, and a polynomial address universe of initially zero cells. Accessed cells and operations are charged; no linear-space or constant-extra-space restriction is imposed. This allows direct tuple-membership tables without charging for touching every unused address. Membership in the target class means that for this fixed q there are an enumerator and constants \(C_{q},B_{q}\) whose preprocessing takes at most \(C_{q} N\) steps, whose word length is at most \(B_{q} \log _{2}(N+2)\), and whose time to the first answer, between consecutive answers, and from the last answer to termination is at most \(C_{q}\) after preprocessing. Empty output must be reported within the same delay bound. Output order is arbitrary and each tuple appears exactly once. The classifier takes q, not D, as input and must halt on every query; it has no prescribed runtime bound and need not output the enumerator. This is an explicit effective yes/no formulation of the source’s broader request for a complete tractability classification. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) (or \(\Theta (\log  N)\) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
why: A missing general tractability boundary for relational query evaluation, connecting logical syntax, enumeration algorithms and fine-grained lower bounds.

importance.reason: A central database-theory classification question: identify exactly which fixed queries permit optimal preprocessing and delay, including the self-joins excluded by classical dichotomies.

progress.text: Bagan–Durand–Grandjean establish the free-connex framework and conditional enumeration dichotomies for the classical acyclic setting.
Carmeli–Segoufin demonstrate additional tractable self-join queries, prove partial classifications and give mirror-query algorithms; preprint 2022, PODS 2023.
Rouvroy’s preliminary research report gives further sufficient and necessary conditions for acyclic self-join queries with binary or unary atoms, leaving examples unclassified.
Chmielewski–Draghici–Olteanu–Zhang study semiring-dependent incremental maintenance and obtain a dichotomy in a self-join-free insert-only setting; this is a different model.

status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The checked primary sources leave the general self-join classification unresolved. The exact target is an editorial effective formulation, with a specified RAM and permissive polynomial memory. Known negative classifications use stated fine-grained hypotheses; newer projected-query and dynamic results do not cover the whole class.

context_blocks.text: A conjunctive query combines relational lookups with shared variables, then projects away variables that are not requested in the output. For example, \(q(x,z)=\exists y R(x,y)\land S(y,z)\) asks for all endpoint pairs connected through an intermediate value. It may have many witnesses y for one answer \((x,z)\), but under the set semantics here that answer must be printed only once. A self-join occurs when several atoms use the same relation symbol.

This is data complexity: q is fixed while the database grows. Even a fixed query can produce quadratically or cubically many answers, so linear total running time is often impossible just because of output size. Linear preprocessing followed by constant delay is a more appropriate ideal. It permits total time proportional to input plus output while also controlling the wait for each answer, including the first one and the final termination signal.

The classical positive condition is free-connex acyclicity. Form the query hypergraph with a vertex for each variable and one edge for the variables of each atom. It is acyclic when its edges admit a join tree: the edges containing any particular variable form a connected subtree. Free-connex additionally requires acyclicity after adding one edge containing all output variables. Bagan–Durand–Grandjean develop constant-delay enumeration for this structure.

For the example \(\exists y R(x,y)\land S(y,z)\), the two atom edges form a path, but adding the output edge \(\{x,z\}\) creates a cycle. Its answers are exactly the nonzero entries in the Boolean product of the two relation matrices. This explains why projection is tied to matrix multiplication. Classical hardness for acyclic self-join-free queries relies on a Boolean-matrix-multiplication assumption, rather than an unconditional superlinear lower bound.

Carmeli–Segoufin show that the self-join-free classification does not extend merely by ignoring repeated relation names. Some cyclic queries with self-joins allow constant-delay enumeration. Their paper gives positive and negative conditions, a classification for queries with at most two output variables under stated hyperclique assumptions, and further results for queries whose Boolean cores are cyclic. A general classification remains outside these theorems.

A particularly instructive example is the full query \(R(x,y)\land R(y,z)\land R(x,t)\land R(t,z)\). A two-step path from x to z already yields an answer with \(t=y\). When another middle vertex becomes available for those endpoints, it can be paired with previously stored middle vertices to produce further answers. The paper generalizes this symmetry through mirror queries. Its algorithms may store information proportional to the output, which is why this card explicitly allows growing memory.

Adding a predicate on only one of the two middle vertices can break that symmetry. More generally, assignments can identify several query variables with one database element. This is allowed by the syntax; injective matching would be another task. Such identifications generate extra answers that can invalidate a hardness reduction designed for independent relations. Any complete criterion has to account for the interaction between repeated symbols, variable identifications and the chosen output variables.

Rouvroy’s May 2025 research report studies acyclic queries with self-joins and projections, focusing on atoms of arity at most two. It develops a sufficient condition through a construction called patching, alongside necessary conditions and examples not captured by either side. The report explicitly says it is not yet polished. These are useful additional tractability results, but the report does not claim the full classification; relation arity at most two also differs from having at most two output variables.

The source question asks for a structural classification. To make this card a definite yes/no problem, the formal target asks whether membership in the tractable class is decidable from query syntax. This does not demand a fast classifier, nor one uniform enumerator with constants independent of q. It does demand termination for every query. A finite list of sufficient patterns is progress only if there is also a justified answer for every remaining query.

Recent dichotomies for incremental view maintenance concern another resource tradeoff. Chmielewski–Draghici–Olteanu–Zhang’s June 2026 preprint studies insertions into semiring-annotated databases and classifies a self-join-free setting using acyclicity and p-hierarchy. There the update cost and the semiring affect tractability. Such a dynamic, annotated classification does not resolve static distinct-answer enumeration with arbitrary self-joins.

A solution would explain exactly when a query can be compiled into an output stream with predictable response time after one linear scan of its data. The significance reaches beyond one faster join implementation: it would provide a general language-level boundary for a basic form of relational computation. The explicit memory, projection and duplicate conventions make proposed classifications comparable instead of allowing the target to change between examples.

sentences: A conjunctive query joins relations and projects the resulting assignments to its output variables.
The question asks for a terminating classifier deciding which queries allow linear preprocessing followed by constant-delay enumeration of distinct answers.
Self-joins are allowed, so repeated uses of one relation can create symmetries and dependencies absent from simpler classifications.
A complete answer would identify the exact boundary for efficiently generating query results in this basic language.
The reviewed formulation fixes the RAM and termination conventions, and the classifier itself need not run quickly or output the enumeration algorithm.
